description: ¡Somos un equipo de dos jóvenes entusiastas del espacio listos para asumir el reto "Abandoned but not Forgotten"! Nuestra meta es crear historias creativas e inspiradoras sobre los emblemáticos rovers y equipos que quedaron en la Luna y Marte. Aportamos pasión por la astronomía, la narrativa y el trabajo en equipo. ¡Buscamos integrantes con habilidades en arte digital, edición de video, desarrollo web o audio para darle vida a estas misiones!
summary: Abandoned Droid is a bilingual (English/Spanish) web prototype that introduces school-age learners to spacecraft and equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. Using first-person artifact narration within a 2D pixel-art scene and synthesized space ambience, visitors explore glowing mission points featuring narratives, status notes, and three visual views: digitized pixel art from children’s drawings, original drawings, and real mission imagery. It also includes a downloadable android builder inspired by mission hardware. No classroom studies or measured learning outcomes have been reported.
details:
Executive Summary

The 2D pixel-art scene invites visitors to open glowing mission points. Each story panel combines a mission narrative and a current-status note with three image views: pixel art digitized from children’s drawings, the original drawing, and a real mission image or labeled illustration. Spanish and English are available. A creative android builder lets visitors assemble a character from parts inspired by mission hardware and download the result as an image. Synthesized space ambience supports the experience.

The concept was created by Thiago Nicolás Terán Casahuamán and Luisa María Belén León Cruzado. The children produced the drawings, with support from adult mentors. Karina Elizabeth Casahuamán Palomino is the children’s guardian.

Visit the repository in github: https://github.com/CatLiss1120/Abandoned-Droid

1. Project Description

1.1. What Does It Do?

The application presents short, story-driven introductions to ten mission artifacts. Selecting a glowing point opens a card that identifies the equipment, describes its purpose and discoveries in first person, and summarizes its current status. The content covers lunar missions, Mars missions, and deep-space exploration; this distinction helps avoid presenting every spacecraft as a Mars mission.

•  Moon: Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, Apollo 12 Intrepid, Apollo 15 Falcon, and Surveyor 3.

•  Mars: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, InSight, Ingenuity, and Viking 1.

•  Deep space: Kepler and Pioneer 10.

The story panel offers Pixel Art, Real Photo (or an appropriately labeled illustration/diagram), and Drawing views. The original children’s drawings remain available alongside their pixel-art derivatives.

1.2. How Does It Work?

The frontend is a React single-page application built with Vite. The landing scene positions clickable markers around celestial objects. Choosing a marker sets the selected mission and opens its information panel. The panel reads bilingual strings from the mission data, switches image sources according to the selected view, and displays the mission status. The language control switches the interface and story text between Spanish and English.

The android builder presents selectable components associated with artifacts such as Surveyor 3, Sojourner, InSight, Viking 1, and Ingenuity. The user combines three pieces, previews the assembled pixel-art android, and can export it as a PNG. The ambient tone is synthesized in the browser with the Web Audio API; browser autoplay restrictions may require a first interaction before sound begins.

1.3. Innovation and Purpose

The central design choice is to treat off-world hardware as a narrator. First-person storytelling links a machine’s construction and mission role to scientific results and the fact that it may remain on a planetary surface or continue traveling after its mission. Children’s drawings provide a recognizable creative layer: pixel-art versions are derived from the drawings, while the unmodified originals and mission imagery remain separate views.

The purpose is to make mission history approachable to school-age and casual audiences, encourage curiosity about robotics and planetary science, and give learners a small creative activity after exploring the stories.

1.4. Benefits and Impact

A. Social, Environmental, and Technological Benefits

•  Social and educational: a free browser experience with Spanish and English text, short narratives, and an accessible entry point for classroom discussion.

•  Environmental: the project does not model or measure environmental impacts; its subject is the scientific exploration of the Moon, Mars, and deep space.

•  Technological: introduces mission hardware, robotic exploration, scientific instruments, web-based interaction, bilingual interface design, and pixel-art image processing.

B. Contribution to the SDGs and Space Missions

The project can support SDG 4 (Quality Education) by providing an informal digital learning resource. This is an intended contribution, not an evaluated outcome or formal SDG certification. Its subject aligns with NASA’s planetary exploration and science communication work by interpreting historical mission artifacts and their scientific contributions.

C. Expected Community Impact

The intended audience is school-age learners, families, educators, and casual space enthusiasts. The experience can support guided discussion about how spacecraft land, move, measure, communicate, and stop operating.

1.5. Objectives and Expected Results

Main objective: create an engaging, accurate, story-driven educational web experience that helps young learners understand selected space hardware and the science it enabled.

•  Present ten artifacts grouped by destination and mission context.

•  Explain each artifact’s role and current status in first-person bilingual stories.

•  Credit and display the children’s drawings while offering pixel-art and mission-image views.

•  Invite exploration through clickable markers and a downloadable android-building activity.

Current result: an interactive prototype deployed on Vercel. The short project demonstration video with English descriptive narration is planned for a later stage.

1.6. Methodology and Work Plan

The project followed these sequential phases:


Main Activities by Stage

•  Translate mission history into short first-person narratives and bilingual interface text.

•  Associate each drawing and pixel-art image with its matching mission point by filename.

•  Keep original sketches and mission photographs/illustrations available as distinct views.

•  Implement the android component selector and PNG export.

•  Publish the web application and document sources, limitations, and future work.

Intermediate Deliverables

•  Mission-story data and current-status descriptions in Spanish and English.

•  Original child-drawn images and pixel-art derivatives stored as web assets.

•  Interactive React interface and CSS animations.

•  Synthesized browser ambience and android builder.

•  Vercel deployment and this technical documentation.

Mission Inventory and Status

1.7. Methodology and Tools

1.7.1. Tools and Software Used

•  Visual Studio Code: project editing environment.

•  React and Vite: user interface and development/build tooling.

•  HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: page structure, styling, state, interactions, and animations.

•  Web Audio API: synthesized ambient sound in the browser.

•  Vercel: hosting and deployment platform.

•  GitHub: source-code repository and deployment source, as reported by the project owner.

1.7.2. Programming Languages and Framework

The project uses JavaScript with React. Vite serves the application during development and generates the production build. HTML provides the page document and CSS supplies the pixel-art presentation, responsive layout, image frames, and animations. The application uses local image assets under the public directory. It is not a data-connected simulation and does not depend on live NASA APIs.

1.7.3. Hardware and Sensors

No physical hardware or sensors are integrated into the application. A computer, tablet, or smartphone with a modern web browser and internet access is sufficient to visit the deployed site. All visual effects, audio, and interactions are software-based.

1.8. Project Management

The children developed the idea and artwork with help from adult mentors. Karina Elizabeth Casahuamán Palomino is the children’s guardian.

1.9. Project Location and Setting

The team is based in Peru. The project is a digital experience hosted at https://abandoned-droid-delta.vercel.app/. It has no physical site or simulated Mars outpost. The web format makes it accessible through standard browsers, subject to internet availability.

1.10. Impact and Benefits: NASA Relevance

The challenge asks participants to explain what equipment remains on the Moon, Mars, and elsewhere and connect that hardware to the missions it enabled. Abandoned Droid addresses this by separating lunar artifacts, Mars explorers, and deep-space spacecraft, then linking each narrative to mission roles and discoveries. NASA is cited as the source for historical and scientific facts; the project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

1.11. Expected Results

•  A deployed bilingual interactive web experience for school-age and casual audiences.

•  Ten mission artifacts with first-person stories, status information, and image views.

•  Pixel-art interpretations linked to the children’s drawings.

•  An android builder that allows a user to combine mission-inspired parts and download an image.

•  A future short video with English descriptive narration; not yet produced.

1.12. Conclusions and Future Improvements

Abandoned Droid turns historical mission hardware into approachable narrators and combines mission information with children’s artwork. Its current contribution is an educational prototype rather than a validated teaching intervention. Future evaluation with students and educators will be needed to assess clarity, accessibility, factual understanding, and classroom usefulness.

Lessons Learned

•  Mission objects must be carefully matched to their destination and actual role.

•  A filename-based artwork mapping helps keep each child’s drawing with the corresponding story.

•  Mission facts and fictional first-person voice should remain distinct: the narrator format is creative, while the technical claims require reliable sources.

•  A browser-based prototype can combine stories, images, language controls, audio, and creative interaction without physical sensors.

Possible Future Improvements

•  Produce the planned short demonstration video with English descriptive narration.

•  Review all mission facts, image captions, and status wording with mentors and educators.

•  Test the site with students and improve accessibility, mobile layouts, and reduced-motion/audio controls based on feedback.

•  Add citations or source links directly in each story panel if desired.

•  Collect non-identifying educational feedback and document results before claiming learning impact.
